issues.subcategory: confound between perception and memory not fully resolved
issues.description: The authors argue that increasing illusions over time proves memory (not perceptual) origin. However, this logic is incomplete. If perceptual encoding is probabilistic and noisy, a participant who initially encoded the pseudo-letter correctly might still have a degraded trace that is later 'corrected' by priors—but this is indistinguishable from a scenario where some trials were misperceived from the start and those misperceptions are simply more likely to be reported with high confidence at longer delays (because correct traces have decayed, leaving only the misperceived ones). The temporal increase in illusions is consistent with memory-based reshaping but does not definitively rule out that a subset of trials were misperceived at encoding and that the proportion of such trials in the high-confidence pool grows as correct memories decay.
issues.quote: If the frequency of reported illusions increases over time, then at least part of the illusions can be attributed to memory processing rather than perceptual encoding.

issues.subcategory: absence of immediate (0 ms delay) baseline
issues.description: To properly establish that illusions increase over time, a true baseline at or near 0 ms delay (e.g., simultaneous probe) is needed. The shortest delay used is 500–750 ms, which is already well beyond iconic memory duration (<500 ms). Any illusions present at 500 ms could already reflect post-perceptual memory processes. Without a 0 ms or very short (<100 ms) baseline, the claim that illusions 'arise' in STM rather than being present from the moment of encoding cannot be fully supported.
issues.quote: In all experiments participants see memory displays that contain both real letters, with the standard orientation, and pseudo-letters, which were mirrored... These experiments test whether STM is susceptible to illusory memories, even when the visual information has only just disappeared, and the perceptual memory trace should still be intact

issues.subcategory: online data collection without experimental control (Experiment 4)
issues.description: Experiment 4 was conducted online via Zoom and Neurotask, with participants using their own laptops. This introduces uncontrolled variability in display timing, screen refresh rates, ambient lighting, screen size, viewing distance, and potential distractions. These factors are particularly critical for a paradigm relying on 250 ms stimulus presentations and precise timing of memory delays. The authors do not report any checks on timing accuracy or screen calibration, making it impossible to verify that the stimulus durations and delays were as specified.
issues.quote: the data was collected in an online experiment, using Neurotask scripting. Participants that signed up to take part in the experiment were invited to join a Zoom meeting at a preset time. Here, each participant was placed in a Zoom break-out room, and given the link to the Neurotask experiment, which they then started on their own laptop.

issues.subcategory: large and unexplained participant exclusion rate
issues.description: In Experiment 2, 92 out of 290 participants (31.7%) were excluded for having fewer than 10 high-confidence trials in one or more cells. This is a very high exclusion rate and raises concerns about selection bias: participants who are excluded are systematically those with fewer high-confidence responses, meaning the included sample is biased toward participants who respond with high confidence more often. This could inflate the apparent rate of high-confidence illusions. The authors do not test whether excluded and included participants differ on other relevant variables, nor do they conduct sensitivity analyses.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) resulted in an inclusion of 198 participants (92 participants were excluded) when the results were averaged across the two color conditions.

issues.subcategory: inconsistent exclusion criteria across experiments
issues.description: The exclusion threshold (minimum 10 high-confidence trials per cell) is applied across all experiments, but the number of trials per cell differs across experiments (different set sizes, number of blocks, and conditions). This means the threshold represents different proportions of trials in different experiments, making the exclusion criterion inconsistent and potentially introducing differential selection bias across experiments.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (5 participants were excluded)... Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) resulted in an inclusion of 198 participants (92 participants were excluded)

issues.subcategory: circular/post-hoc exclusion based on dependent variable
issues.description: Participants are excluded based on having too few high-confidence trials. High confidence is the dependent variable of interest (the study focuses on high-confidence errors). Excluding participants based on a threshold of the dependent variable introduces circularity: the analysis is restricted to participants who show the behavior of interest (high confidence responding), which could artificially inflate effect sizes and bias the results toward the hypotheses.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis

issues.subcategory: no correction for multiple comparisons in follow-up tests
issues.description: Multiple follow-up t-tests and ANOVAs are conducted after the main Bayesian ANOVA (e.g., separate ANOVAs for illusory vs. non-illusory errors, follow-up t-tests comparing short vs. long delays). No correction for multiple comparisons is applied or discussed. While Bayesian analyses do not require correction in the same way as frequentist tests, the authors mix Bayesian and frequentist language and do not acknowledge the inflated false-positive risk from multiple tests.
issues.quote: Follow-up ANOVAs conducted separately for each error type showed that for illusory errors, the optimal model consisted of the factors Memory delay, Target type and the interaction between the two

issues.subcategory: sequential stopping rule not pre-registered and BF threshold differs across experiments
issues.description: Experiments 3 and 4 use sequential Bayes Factor stopping rules, but the BF threshold differs between experiments (BF=6 for Experiment 3, BF=10 for Experiment 4). The authors do not explain why different thresholds were used, nor do they report whether these stopping rules were pre-registered. Sequential testing without pre-registration and with inconsistent stopping criteria raises concerns about researcher degrees of freedom and inflated Type I error rates.
issues.quote: once the outcome crossed a BF of 6, testing would stop... once the outcome crossed a BF of 10, testing would stop.

issues.subcategory: Bayesian ANOVA applied to proportions without transformation
issues.description: The dependent variable is a proportion (error rate), which is bounded between 0 and 1 and is unlikely to be normally distributed, especially at extreme values. The Bayesian repeated-measures ANOVA assumes normally distributed residuals. No transformation (e.g., arcsine, logit) is reported, and no justification is given for applying a normal-assumption model to proportion data. This could affect the validity of the statistical inferences.
issues.quote: The resulting data were analysed in a Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA in JASP 0.16.4, with the factors Target Type (real or pseudo-letter), Memory Delay (short, short with interference and long) and Error Type.

issues.subcategory: BFincl interpretation without reporting posterior distributions or effect sizes
issues.description: The authors report Bayes Factors for inclusion (BFincl) but do not report posterior distributions, credible intervals, or standardized effect sizes for any of the key comparisons. BFincl values alone do not convey the magnitude or precision of effects, making it difficult to assess practical significance or compare effect sizes across experiments.
issues.quote: Hypothesis 1 was supported: Illusions (pseudo-to-real or real-to-pseudo) were much more prevalent than other errors (a main effect of Error Type, BFincl>1000).

issues.subcategory: response bias not adequately controlled
issues.description: The authors dismiss response bias as an explanation by stating 'the pattern of responses across conditions is consistent with memory-driven processes rather than response bias,' but this is not a formal test. A response bias toward selecting real letters (regardless of memory) would produce exactly the pattern observed: more pseudo-to-real than real-to-pseudo errors, and this bias could increase over time as memory fades and participants fall back on default responding. The authors do not include a condition where no memory display is shown (pure response bias baseline) to quantify the baseline tendency to select real over pseudo letters.
issues.quote: Yet another reason why illusory reports arise could be a response bias: Participant might just be more inclined to select real letters instead of pseudo-letters, since real letters are a well-known category. However, this is unlikely because the pattern of responses across conditions is consistent with memory-driven processes rather than response bias.

issues.subcategory: unbalanced trial proportions in Experiments 1 and 2
issues.description: In Experiment 1, real letter targets make up 75% of trials and pseudo-letter targets 25%. In Experiment 2, pseudo-letters make up 33% of targets. This imbalance means participants have more experience with real letter targets throughout the experiment, which could create an experiment-induced response bias independent of world knowledge. While Experiments 3 and 4 address this, the authors' conclusions from Experiments 1 and 2 regarding world knowledge as the driver are weakened by this confound.
issues.quote: The target letter was a real letter in 75% of the trials and a pseudo-letter in the remaining 25%.

issues.subcategory: failure of Experiment 2 manipulation check for cue color
issues.description: The cue color manipulation (intended to induce transient expectations about real vs. pseudo-letter targets) had no effect on illusion rates. The authors conclude that 'expectations need substantial time to develop before they can affect explicit, high confidence memories.' However, they do not verify that participants learned the cue-target contingency. No manipulation check (e.g., questionnaire about cue meaning, or analysis of accuracy as a function of cue validity) is reported. Without evidence that participants processed the cue as informative, the null result is uninterpretable.
issues.quote: The relationship between the colour of the cue and the nature of the target was not mentioned in any of the responses.

issues.subcategory: interference display confound
issues.description: The 'Short with Interference' condition in Experiment 1 introduces a second letter display that contains real and pseudo-letters. This display could itself trigger letter-related expectations and prime real-letter responses, confounding the interference effect (memory decay) with a priming effect (activation of real-letter representations). The authors do not control for or discuss this alternative explanation.
issues.quote: the second letter display appeared together with the cue... This display consisted of randomly selected letters, unrelated to the memory display.

issues.subcategory: training task differs from experimental task
issues.description: In Experiment 1, participants were trained on a cued change detection task using oriented rectangles, not letters. The training task is fundamentally different from the experimental task (letter identification). The training serves to select participants with good visual memory, but it is unclear whether performance on the rectangle task predicts performance on the letter task, or whether the training itself introduces any systematic biases.
issues.quote: Prior to the main experiment, participants were trained on a cued change detection task. In this training task, participants were instructed to indicate whether the rectangle at a cued location in a memory display had the same orientation as the rectangle at that same location in a test display.

issues.subcategory: generalizability limited to letters
issues.description: All four experiments use letters of the alphabet as stimuli. The authors claim that 'world knowledge' drives STM illusions, but the specific stimuli (letters) are highly overlearned, linguistically meaningful, and have strong verbal codes. The findings may not generalize to other visual stimuli or to world knowledge in general. The authors briefly mention this in the discussion (referencing Chalk et al.) but do not adequately caveat the generalizability of their conclusions.
issues.quote: All experiments rely on the extensive experience participants have with the alphabet. Previous experience with letters should have provided participants with abundant evidence that letters typically appear in their standard form.

issues.subcategory: verbal recoding confound
issues.description: Letters are highly susceptible to verbal recoding: participants may verbally rehearse the letter name (e.g., 'C') rather than maintaining a visual representation. If participants verbally recode the pseudo-letter as its real counterpart at encoding (e.g., seeing 'Ɔ' and thinking 'C'), then the illusion is a perceptual/encoding phenomenon, not a memory phenomenon. The authors do not include an articulatory suppression condition to prevent verbal recoding, which would be a critical control.
issues.quote: FTT does suggest that pseudo-letters have a verbal (the letter itself) and a gist level ('mirrored') representation, while real letters can be stored purely at the verbal level... Removing verbal rehearsal as a strategy, for example through articulatory suppression, would therefore impact the storage of the verbal representation in working memory

issues.subcategory: confidence scale differences across experiments
issues.description: Experiment 1 uses a 2-point confidence scale (1=guess, 2=certain), while Experiments 2, 3, and 4 use a 4-point confidence scale (1-4). The definition of 'high confidence' therefore differs across experiments (score of 2 in Experiment 1 vs. presumably scores of 3-4 in later experiments, though this is not explicitly stated). This makes direct quantitative comparisons of high-confidence error rates across experiments problematic.
issues.quote: After selecting the target letter, participants indicated their confidence by clicking on one of two boxes (from 1-2, 1 = guess, 2 = certain)... participants first chose the target letter from 6 different response options, and then indicated her confidence (on a scale from 1 - 4).

issues.subcategory: high confidence threshold not defined for 4-point scale
issues.description: For Experiments 2, 3, and 4, which use a 4-point confidence scale, the authors never explicitly define what constitutes 'high confidence.' It is unclear whether high confidence means a rating of 4 only, 3 or 4, or some other threshold. This omission makes the analyses non-reproducible and prevents readers from evaluating whether the threshold choice affects the results.
issues.quote: participants first chose the target letter from 6 different response options, and then indicated her confidence (on a scale from 1 - 4).

issues.subcategory: missing descriptive statistics
issues.description: Throughout the results sections, the authors report mean error rates but do not consistently report measures of variability (standard deviations, standard errors, or credible intervals) for the key dependent variables. This makes it impossible to assess the precision of the estimates or to conduct independent power calculations.
issues.quote: Illusory memories make up almost 20% of reports when memory is probed at 500 ms (Experiment 1 and 2) and up to 30% of reports when memory is probed at 3 seconds (Experiment 1-4).

issues.subcategory: figure numbering error
issues.description: Experiment 4 references 'Figure 5' for its results ('Figure 5 shows the error rates for high confidence trials'), but Figure 5 was already used for Experiment 3. The figure for Experiment 4 results is labeled Figure 6 in the caption. This is an internal inconsistency that creates confusion about which figure presents which data.
issues.quote: Figure 5 shows the error rates for high confidence trials. A Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA model comparison showed that the model with main effects for Error Type, Target Type, Memory Delay...

issues.subcategory: typo in BFincl label
issues.description: In the Experiment 2 results, the authors write 'BFinlc>1000' (transposed letters), which is a typographical error. While minor, it reduces the professionalism and clarity of the manuscript.
issues.quote: Participants were more likely to select the mirrored (pseudo) counterpart of a target than to commit other types of errors (18% vs 11%, main effect of error type, BFinlc>1000)

issues.subcategory: missing pre-registration information
issues.description: The authors do not mention whether any of the four experiments were pre-registered. Given that the study involves multiple experiments with sequential stopping rules, post-hoc exclusion criteria, and multiple dependent variables, the absence of pre-registration (or a statement about its absence) is a significant transparency issue.
issues.quote: Here we report 4 experiments that test whether STM is susceptible to illusory memories.

issues.subcategory: appendix referenced but not provided
issues.description: The authors repeatedly reference 'Appendix 1' for full model comparisons, but no appendix is included in the manuscript as provided. This makes it impossible to verify the model comparison results or assess whether the best-fitting model was selected appropriately.
issues.quote: see Appendix 1 for full model comparison and Table 1 for an overview of BFincl for each model component

issues.subcategory: model selection based on BFm without reporting all competing models
issues.description: The authors select the best-fitting model based on BFm (posterior model odds) but only report the winning model and the BFincl for individual components. The full model comparison table is relegated to an appendix that is not provided. Without seeing all competing models and their BFm values, it is impossible to assess whether the model selection was appropriate or whether alternative models with similar fit were considered.
issues.quote: The Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA showed that a model with main effects for Error Type, Target Type, and Memory Delay, and a Target Type * Error Type and Memory Delay * Error Type interaction had the best fit (BFm = 18, see Appendix 1 for full model comparison

issues.subcategory: sample heterogeneity across experiments
issues.description: Experiments 1 uses a small, highly selected sample (n=40 after training, n=23 after exclusion) recruited for monetary compensation. Experiments 2-4 use large samples of first-year psychology students participating for course credit. These populations differ in motivation, cognitive ability screening, and familiarity with experimental tasks. The authors do not discuss how this heterogeneity might affect the comparability of results across experiments.
issues.quote: 45 participants started training, 5 participants were excluded based on their training results. The remaining 40 participants... In this experiment, 290 participants took part... The participants participated for student credits as part of a course within the first-year Psychology curriculum.

issues.subcategory: no control for individual differences in letter knowledge or reading ability
issues.description: The study relies on participants having strong prior knowledge of the standard letter forms. However, no measure of reading ability, language background, or letter familiarity is collected. Participants with dyslexia, non-native alphabet users, or those with weaker letter representations might show different patterns. This is particularly relevant given the diverse age range (17-56 years) in Experiment 2.
issues.quote: All experiments rely on the extensive experience participants have with the alphabet.

issues.subcategory: stimulus size reported in inconsistent or potentially erroneous units
issues.description: In the training section, rectangles are described as '0.05° × 0.01° in size,' which are extremely small visual angles (approximately 0.9 × 0.2 arcminutes). These dimensions seem implausibly small for stimuli that participants are expected to identify and remember. This may be a reporting error (possibly pixels or cm rather than degrees of visual angle), which would affect the replicability of the study.
issues.quote: The memory and test displays each consisted of eight white rectangles (0.05◦ × 0.01◦ in size)

issues.subcategory: no measure of awareness of pseudo-letter manipulation
issues.description: Participants are instructed not to confuse real and pseudo-letters, but no measure is taken of whether participants understood the distinction, could reliably identify pseudo-letters, or were aware of the mirroring manipulation. Without such a check, it is unclear whether the illusions reflect a failure of awareness of the pseudo-letter status or a genuine memory transformation.
issues.quote: Participants were instructed to report the letter that appeared at the cued location. They were explicitly instructed not to confuse real and pseudo-letters and received feedback on their performance after each trial.

issues.subcategory: conflation of STM subtypes
issues.description: The authors claim their findings apply to STM in general and specifically to working memory and fragile memory stages. However, the experimental paradigm (250 ms display, 500 ms–3 s delay, cued recall) is most consistent with fragile memory or early working memory. The authors do not test iconic memory (which would require <500 ms delays) and cannot make strong claims about whether illusions arise in iconic memory. The discussion conflates these distinct STM subtypes.
issues.quote: Our findings suggest that illusory memories can occur during the WM and FM stages of STM... Our experiments currently do not test whether illusory memories arise in IM

issues.subcategory: alternative explanation of familiarity-based responding not fully addressed
issues.description: An alternative to predictive processing is that participants use familiarity as a retrieval cue: when the memory trace is weak, they select the response option that feels most familiar, and real letters are more familiar than pseudo-letters. This is distinct from both response bias and predictive processing, and would predict the same pattern of results. The authors do not discuss or rule out this familiarity-based account.
issues.quote: Instead 'world knowledge' (e.g., which orientation letters usually have) appear to drive these STM illusions.

issues.subcategory: predictive processing framework not uniquely supported
issues.description: The authors favor a predictive processing interpretation but acknowledge that other frameworks (e.g., fuzzy trace theory, familiarity-based memory) could also account for the data. The predictive processing account is not uniquely supported by the data—the results are consistent with any framework that predicts stronger priors for real letters leading to more pseudo-to-real errors. The authors do not design any experiment to specifically test predictions unique to predictive processing versus alternatives.
issues.quote: One possibility is that both perception and cognitive processes such as STM operate according to Bayesian principles. According to these principles, as expressed in frameworks such as 'predictive processing', top-down prior expectations are integrated with bottom-up input to form perceptual or cognitive content.

issues.subcategory: no eye-tracking or fixation control
issues.description: The experiments use stimuli presented around a fixation point, but no eye-tracking is used to verify that participants maintained fixation during the 250 ms memory display. Eye movements toward specific letters during encoding could systematically affect which items are better encoded, potentially confounding the results. This is particularly relevant given that pseudo-letters may attract more attention due to their novelty.
issues.quote: The memory display consisted of 6 or 8 letters... Individual rectangles were evenly distributed on an imaginary circle (radius 4.68◦) around fixation.

issues.subcategory: cue validity and its effect on memory not analyzed
issues.description: In Experiment 1, the cue appears either 100 ms or 1 second after memory display offset. The authors do not analyze whether cue timing affects illusion rates, even though earlier cueing might allow participants to selectively rehearse the cued item, potentially reducing illusions. This is a potentially important variable that is not reported.
issues.quote: The cue appeared either 100 milliseconds, or 1 second after offset of the memory display.

issues.subcategory: incomplete reporting of accuracy rates
issues.description: The paper focuses exclusively on error rates in high-confidence trials but does not report overall accuracy rates (including low-confidence trials) or d-prime measures. Without overall accuracy, it is impossible to assess whether the high-confidence error rates are meaningful relative to overall performance, or whether the confidence manipulation is working as intended.
issues.quote: For each memory delay (short, short with interference and long) and each target type (pseudo- and real letter targets) the occurrence of illusory errors (real-to-pseudo or pseudo-to-real errors) and other errors (selection of one of the unrelated distractor items) was calculated.

issues.subcategory: prior specification for Bayesian ANOVA not reported
issues.description: The authors use Bayesian repeated-measures ANOVAs in JASP but do not report the prior distributions used (e.g., Cauchy prior scale for effect sizes). The default JASP priors may not be appropriate for all comparisons, and the choice of prior can substantially affect Bayes Factors, especially for small effects. Without reporting the priors, the analyses are not fully reproducible.
issues.quote: The resulting data were analysed in a Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA in JASP 0.16.4

issues.subcategory: mixing of Bayesian and frequentist language
issues.description: The authors use Bayesian ANOVAs as the primary analysis but then conduct follow-up 't-tests' (presumably frequentist) without reporting p-values or test statistics, only Bayes Factors. The mixing of frameworks without clear justification, and the use of 't-test' terminology in a Bayesian context, is confusing and methodologically inconsistent.
issues.quote: Illusory responses increased from 14% to 19% in the longer delays (BF > 1000 in follow-up t-test), while the other non-illusory error rate only increased from 6% to 7% (BF = 4.84 in a follow up t-test).

issues.subcategory: set size confound in Experiment 1
issues.description: Experiment 1 uses memory displays of either 6 or 8 letters, with different numbers of pseudo-letters depending on set size. The authors state results are 'averaged across the set size conditions' without reporting whether set size affects illusion rates. Set size is a known moderator of working memory performance and could interact with the illusion effects.
issues.quote: When the memory display consisted of 8 letters, it contained 2 pseudo-letters. When it contained 6 letters, it had a 50% chance of containing 1 pseudo-letter and a 50% chance of containing 2 pseudo-letters.

issues.subcategory: causal language used without causal design
issues.description: Throughout the paper, the authors use causal language (e.g., 'world knowledge drives STM illusions,' 'expectations reshape perceptual representations,' 'prior expectations can shape memory traces'). However, the design is correlational/observational—no manipulation directly controls world knowledge or prior strength. The asymmetry between pseudo-to-real and real-to-pseudo errors is consistent with world knowledge effects but does not prove causation.
issues.quote: Instead 'world knowledge' (e.g., which orientation letters usually have) appear to drive these STM illusions.

issues.subcategory: no measure of subjective experience of illusion
issues.description: The study claims to demonstrate 'memory illusions'—cases where participants have a subjective experience of remembering something that was not there. However, the study only measures behavioral responses and confidence ratings. There is no phenomenological measure (e.g., 'remember/know' judgments, source monitoring questions) to verify that high-confidence errors reflect genuine illusory recollective experiences rather than high-confidence guesses or familiarity-based responses.
issues.quote: Focusing on memory illusions instead of general false memory reports allows a separation of such incorrect but seemingly true memories from memory lapses that are filled in by best guesses

issues.subcategory: feedback during experiment may shape expectations
issues.description: Participants receive trial-by-trial feedback on their performance throughout the experiments. This feedback could itself shape participants' expectations about the prevalence of real vs. pseudo-letter targets, potentially creating experiment-induced biases that confound the world-knowledge manipulation. The authors do not discuss or control for this.
issues.quote: They were explicitly instructed not to confuse real and pseudo-letters and received feedback on their performance after each trial.

issues.subcategory: inconsistent description of Experiment 4 results figure
issues.description: The text of Experiment 4 results states 'Figure 5 shows the error rates for high confidence trials' but the actual figure for Experiment 4 is labeled Figure 6 in the caption. This is a clear error that could mislead readers.
issues.quote: Figure 5 shows the error rates for high confidence trials.

issues.subcategory: no independent replication within the same lab
issues.description: While the paper presents four experiments, each experiment differs from the others in multiple ways (sample size, confidence scale, set size, online vs. lab, balanced vs. unbalanced stimuli). None of the experiments is a direct replication of another. The progressive changes across experiments make it difficult to attribute differences in effect sizes to specific design changes.
issues.quote: Here we report 4 experiments that test whether STM is susceptible to illusory memories.

issues.subcategory: BFincl values reported as greater than 1000 without exact values
issues.description: Many Bayes Factors are reported as '>1000' or '∞' without exact values. While these indicate very strong evidence, reporting exact values (or at least order-of-magnitude estimates) would be more informative and transparent, particularly for comparing effect sizes across experiments and conditions.
issues.quote: Illusions (pseudo-to-real or real-to-pseudo) were much more prevalent than other errors (a main effect of Error Type, BFincl>1000)
